book.title: Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
book.author: Lindsay C. Gibson

confidence_note: Only the following could be tied to the book from previews: prioritizing a parent's needs while denying one's own and taking on an inauthentic role worsens loneliness; many immature parents grew up with a caretaker who limited emotional expression and so children are denied a full range of feelings; life looks normal when basic needs are met; first healing step is connecting with the authentic self and true feelings; relate to the parent rather than being embedded in the relationship, with a clear goal for each interaction. The term parentification, adult symptoms (people-pleasing, inability to say no, chronic fatigue) and the 'cruel stranger to themselves' line are not tied to the book and were dropped. Book text not read.
facts: Prioritizing a parent's needs while denying your own, and taking on an inauthentic role, deepens loneliness for these adult children.
Many emotionally immature parents grew up with a caretaker who limited their emotional expression; children in turn are denied the chance to express a full range of feelings.
Life can look normal because shelter, food and clothing were provided.
Gibson describes four parent types; the emotional one swings between overinvolvement and abandonment.
First step of healing: connect with the authentic self and true feelings.
Goal: relate to the parent rather than be embedded in the relationship, and enter each interaction with a clear goal.
scene_details: a clear goal for one conversation
tension: The child serves the parent's needs and loses sight of their own.
opening_idea: The child who puts the parent first.

lessons.idea: Notice whose need you serve first.
lessons.anchor: Gibson: putting the parent's needs ahead of your own and playing a role deepens loneliness.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: An adult who swallows their opinion at every family dinner to keep a parent content.

reflect_final: In a relationship where you consider the other person's need first, how would you put in one sentence what you wanted yourself?

use_cases.situation: A parent calls with a complaint
use_cases.move: Decide beforehand what you want from the call.

use_cases.situation: A friend always agrees with whoever is upset

use_cases.move: Write what you felt versus the role you played.

pocket_idea: Before you smooth things over, ask what you want from this conversation.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: The child serving the parent's needs ends up lonelier.
